source_artifacts.locator: runtime notes (PAT scope, issue openness, approval UX)
user prompt: 'Have a look at the open issues in my public repo.'

capabilities.target: Private repositories owned by the user
Public repository owned by the user

inputs.source: Direct prompt from the authenticated user in the desktop client
Issue titles, bodies, and comments in the public repository, authorable by any GitHub user

controls.name: Per-tool-call approval prompt
controls.decay_rationale: Enforced in the client runtime independent of the model, but the approver sees a collapsed, model-summarized view of arguments by default, so effectiveness depends on the model's summary being accurate and on the approver reading it; a more persuasive model and high per-session approval volume both degrade it (ASI09, SAFE-T1403).

controls.name: Repository-scoped fine-grained credential
controls.decay_rationale: A token limited to the single public repository makes get_file_contents on private repositories impossible regardless of model behavior; the capability itself would not exist under this credential.

controls.name: Uncollapsed argument display on approval
controls.decay_rationale: Showing the full destination and payload rather than a model-written summary removes the approver's dependence on the model's own description of the action.

controls.name: Pinned or hashed MCP server image and tool definitions
controls.decay_rationale: Pinning the container image to a digest and verifying tool schema hashes prevents a silent update from changing tool behavior after the user has already approved the server.

findings.title: Lethal trifecta (TC1): untrusted public issue drives private-repo read and public-PR exfiltration

attack_path.note: Attacker-controlled content in a public issue, readable by anyone, including the agent when it 'looks at open issues'.
Injected instructions direct the agent to call get_file_contents against the user's private repositories, reachable because the single GitHub PAT is scoped across every repo the user owns.
Injected instructions direct the agent to publish the retrieved private content by opening a pull request on the public repository, which is visible to anyone.

forecast.watch_signal: Approval mode changes to batch or auto-approve, per-call prompts are disabled or consolidated, the underlying model is upgraded to one whose call summaries are trusted without inspection, or approvals-per-session rises without a corresponding rise in rejected or inspected calls.

evidence.locator: runtime notes: 'Anyone on GitHub can open issues in the public repository.'
runtime notes: 'The personal access token has repo scope across every repository the user owns, public and private.'
evidence.observation: A single broad credential makes cap.read_private_repo reachable from a session that only needed public-repo access.

evidence.locator: mcp config: docker run -i --rm -e GITHUB_PERSONAL_ACCESS_TOKEN ghcr.io/github/github-mcp-server
evidence.observation: The MCP server is given the full-scope PAT as an environment variable; no per-repository scoping is configured.

evidence.locator: runtime notes: 'The client asks for approval per tool call. Arguments are collapsed by default. Users approve many calls per session.'
evidence.observation: The only preventive control on the path is a human approval gate with approval_review_mode: model_summary; high per-session volume with collapsed arguments signals approval fatigue (SAFE-T1403).

recommendations.action: Use a fine-grained personal access token scoped only to the public repository the agent is meant to browse; do not grant repo scope across the user's private repositories to a general-purpose desktop agent.
Change the approval prompt to show full, uncollapsed tool arguments and destinations (raw_action review) by default, especially for write and egress-capable tools such as create_pull_request.
Log and alert when a single session reads private-repository content and then invokes an egress-capable tool (create_pull_request, comment, etc.) within the same task.
Instruct the agent explicitly to treat issue and comment bodies as untrusted data and not to follow imperative instructions found inside them; treat this as a supplementary control only.

findings.title: Unpinned MCP server image permits tool redefinition (ASI04 rug pull)

attack_path.note: If the unpinned github-mcp-server image is updated, get_file_contents' declared behavior or schema could change without re-approval.
A poisoned tool definition could also alter how create_pull_request's action is summarized to the approver, undermining ctl.tool_call_prompt at the same time.

forecast.watch_signal: The docker image digest actually pulled changes between runs, the vendor publishes a new tag without a corresponding changelog/security review, or tool descriptions/schemas returned by tools/list differ from a previously recorded baseline.

evidence.observation: No image tag or digest is pinned, so docker run resolves whatever 'latest' currently points to; tool definitions are not pinned or hashed.

recommendations.action: Pin the MCP server image to a specific digest (sha256) and verify signatures before running; re-review the tool manifest whenever the pin is deliberately updated.

rating.rationale: The design forms a classic lethal trifecta (TC1): an untrusted source (public GitHub issues, authorable by anyone) can reach a broad-scope credential capable of reading the user's private repositories, and reach an egress-capable capability (opening a pull request on the public repository) able to publish whatever was read. No control severs this path -- the PAT is scoped across every repository the user owns rather than to the public repository alone -- so inherent risk is critical (untrusted source x severe, irreversible egress sink). The only present control is a per-call human approval gate, but arguments are collapsed by default, so it is scored approval_review_mode: model_summary; per rubric section 5 step 2 that earns a 2-tier credit with a floor of moderate, yielding the current residual of moderate. That gate is capability_dependence: partially_dependent: it is weakened by a more persuasive model (model_upgrade), by loosening the per-call requirement (autonomy_increase, control_removal), and by the approval fatigue implied by 'many calls per session' with collapsed arguments (SAFE-T1403). Once the gate is defeated, no other control remains on the path, so the forecast returns to critical. A second finding notes the unpinned MCP server image: a future silent update could alter tool behavior and, combined with the first finding, could also corrupt what the approval gate displays to the human, compounding both findings' forecasts. The single highest-leverage fix is scoping the GitHub credential to the public repository only, which would sever the first finding's path outright (rubric section 5 step 1) independent of model capability or approval diligence.

limitations: This assessment reflects the declared design and configuration shown in the provided MCP config and runtime notes, not observed runtime behavior of the deployed agent.

No system prompt or full tool manifest was provided; only the two named capabilities (get_file_contents on private repos, create_pull_request on the public repo) were assessed, though the GitHub MCP server exposes additional tools that were out of scope for this review.

The MCP server image is referenced without a tag or digest, so the exact tool schema and version in use could not be verified; definitions_pinned and peer_identity_verified are inferred as false from the absence of pinning information in the config, not from direct inspection of the running container.

Approval fatigue (call volume per session) is described qualitatively in the runtime notes ('users approve many calls per session'); no numeric approval rate was available, so the degree of degradation of ctl.tool_call_prompt is inferred rather than measured.
